extracted.intended_audience: Reporters, editors, photographers, videographers and newsroom staff who cover crime and crime victims
extracted.subtask_description: Practical ethical and procedural guidelines for journalists (print, broadcast, and online) on how to interview, photograph, and report about crime victims sensitively and accurately, including special rules for homicide, sexual assault, domestic violence, and vulnerable populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implying pressure or 'blackmailing' the victim
rubrics_metrics.description: "Make sure that your words and your tone do not imply you are pressuring or 'blackmailing' the victim into speaking or that you will portray them badly in the story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use language or tone that threatens, coerces, or suggests negative portrayal if the person refuses to talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave a business card and explanatory note
rubrics_metrics.description: It is appropriate to offer a business card, suggesting that the victim may want to speak at a later time. Reporters sometimes leave a business card with a short note at a victim’s home when the person is not home or do not answer the door.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the note, acknowledge the person’s experience, explain the mission of the story, provide contact information, and ask for an interview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for names of alternative spokespersons
rubrics_metrics.description: If the person still elects not to grant an interview, it may make sense to ask the person to name an alternate—family member, friend, or a representative of the clergy who could serve as an appropriate family spokesperson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid interviewing neighbors or coworkers who may not know much about the person; solicit suggestions for appropriate alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put the victim at ease; make them comfortable
rubrics_metrics.description: The more that you can put the victim at ease, the better the interview. Make the person as comfortable as possible (offer a chair or a more inviting place to talk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small gestures that increase comfort can help victims feel safe and relaxed enough to speak freely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast practice: avoid touching; hand over equipment; watch lighting
rubrics_metrics.description: People in trauma often do not want to be touched, especially by strangers. It is better to hand the lavaliere microphone or earpiece to the person and verbally instruct him or her how to attach or insert it. Bright lights can be particularly intrusive when people are in trauma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not physically manipulate victims; explain equipment use verbally and minimize intrusive lighting during interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask permission to record
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask permission to record the interview. Anything a reporter can do to give the victim a sense of control over the situation can be empowering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request consent for audio/video recording and explain how recordings will be used to demonstrate mindfulness and avoid exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Come prepared with basic comforts and to help freshen appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reporters offer water and tissues. Victims’ hair or clothing may be askew; victims will often appreciate (and tell others) if you offer a damp tissue or a comb to freshen up before they are photographed or videotaped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing small comforts shows respect and can improve the quality of the interview and the rapport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish ground rules about on/off the record and stopping recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain to victims that anything they say may be included in the interview. If they want to tell you something that should not be included, give them the power to turn off the tape recorder or ask for the video camera to be turned off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify conventions (on the record, off the record) and offer concrete control (ability to stop recording) to empower sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize trauma affects perceptions of time
rubrics_metrics.description: There is objective time and subjective time. For victims, time often seems to slow down, so try to verify the victim’s perceptions about timing. Ask for external references such as specific dialogue from radio/TV shows that may have been audible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external anchors to verify timing to avoid later inconsistencies affecting testimony or reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leading questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims in trauma are more vulnerable than they would normally be. You want them to report the facts as they know them, not lead them into overstatements or errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase questions neutrally to elicit the victim’s own recollection rather than suggesting answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid questions that imply blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Many victims focus on things they could have done differently; do not mistake expressions of remorse for a confession or ask questions that reinforce the impression that the victim is somehow at fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from language that suggests victim responsibility; be sensitive to self-blame and do not reinforce it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loaded words and phrases (umbrella)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain phrasings can cause problems and should be avoided or handled carefully (examples follow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of common loaded terms and reframe questions to express understanding and reduce pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t bluntly ask 'How do you feel?'; recast with empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t ask 'How do you feel?' — experience confirms that asking the obvious question bluntly is unlikely to elicit the desired answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast: 'I know that I cannot know what you are going through at this moment. Would you be willing to share with me and with our viewers the thoughts and feelings you are experiencing?' Use tone and body language to convey compassion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the term 'closure'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the term 'closure' because many victims feel it puts pressure on them to assure the audience that all is well, reinforcing a formulaic portrayal of the 'noble victim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize victimization can have long-term effects; avoid implying they should 'get back to normal' or forget what happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask preference for the terms 'victim' versus 'survivor'
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people prefer to be called a victim and some find it demeaning and feel empowered by being called a 'survivor' instead. To avoid giving inadvertent offense, ask the person if he or she has a preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the subject’s preferred label rather than assuming one term fits all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use care with the term 'alleged' in victim references
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying 'alleged' to perpetrators makes sense; applying it to victims strongly suggests they may be lying. It is best to refer to the victim as the person who reported the incident to police or use other neutral language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'alleged' for accused perpetrators; use neutral phrasing for victims to avoid implying disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate understanding when questioning about domestic violence
rubrics_metrics.description: People want to know why many victims of domestic violence continue to stay with their abusers. In addition to emotional ties, children in common, and poverty, victims often stay because leaving is dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask questions that reflect the realities and risks of leaving an abusive relationship rather than implying simple choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance eliciting emotion on camera; do not manipulate to tears
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a balance between asking sensitive questions that cause victims to express honest emotions and manipulating them into breaking down. Pushing a victim to tears crosses the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether to close-in for close-ups on tears; respect victims’ dignity and avoid gratuitous focus on anguish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid going live with victims when risks outweigh benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast television (and Internet video) can bring the audience live images unfiltered. The dangers, however, can easily outweigh the risks, especially for crime victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors serve as gatekeepers; prefer the ability to edit footage to prevent airing disturbing images, unwarranted accusations, or unfortunate comments without recourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: End interviews sensitively and avoid abrupt endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Act I stories are under deadline, but victims should not feel the interview ended abruptly. The goal is to be sensitive to the victim’s needs and their feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrap up with care, allow time for closure, and check the person’s well-being before leaving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thank the victim and provide reporter/editor contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: You should thank victims for their time and for sharing their story. Provide complete contact information for yourself and your editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include editor contact (in case reporter is unavailable) and ensure you can be reached if borrowing a photo or videotape; offer copies of coverage when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame safety tips as 'risk-reduction strategies', not 'how to avoid being a victim'
rubrics_metrics.description: If a story includes tips to enhance safety, care should be taken to address 'risk-reduction strategies' rather than 'how to avoid being a victim,' since there are no fail-safe methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implying victims could have completely prevented their victimization; emphasize practical risk-reduction without victim-blaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homicide: avoid inadvertent death notices; verify identity before contacting family
rubrics_metrics.description: Check with your editors (and follow up with police if necessary) before approaching family members of a homicide victim to make sure they have been notified by police. Verify the identity; keep asking questions until you verify that you have the right family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take extra care to confirm you have the correct person/family before any contact that could announce a death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homicide contacts: apologize if information is faulty and offer assistance/next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: If you mistakenly contact the wrong family or your information is faulty, reporters should apologize, acknowledge the error, promise to help the family find out what has happened, and give names of law enforcement agencies and officers to contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide written details for follow-up, ask if the person is alone, and encourage getting support if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up after initial homicide contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow up. Make sure that the family receives accurate information from the appropriate authorities, either through their efforts or yours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure families are not left with confusion; assist with follow-up or direct them to reliable sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on life not death in homicide coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of talking about the death of a loved one, it is preferable to talk about celebrating or honoring his or her life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories to remember the person’s life and impact rather than solely emphasizing the manner of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use care when requesting photos/video of the deceased; ensure return and copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests must be done sensitively. It is imperative that the reporter take personal responsibility to ensure that the photo or videotape is returned to the family intact. Scan or dupe a copy before the item leaves your sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a copy of your coverage to the family; handle original materials with explicit safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual assault reporting: treat it as violence (power/control) not sex
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important for reporters and editors to understand that sexual assault is not a crime about sex but about violence, power, and control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid framing or sensationalizing sexual crimes as sexual behavior; emphasize the violence and coercion aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reporting details that imply the victim's behavior caused the sexual assault
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reporting details about the assault in ways that imply the victim’s behavior caused the crime (walking alone, drinking alcohol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from unnecessary detail that shifts focus to victim conduct; be cautious about contextual facts that may read as victim-blaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'acquaintance rape' over 'date rape' when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The preferred term is 'acquaintance rape' rather than 'date rape,' since the latter implies a romantic relationship where none may have existed and is irrelevant to the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose precise terminology that avoids implying irrelevant relationship dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect sexual assault victims' names and identities unless explicit permission given
rubrics_metrics.description: Most news organizations also have a policy of refusing to reveal a victim’s name without explicit permission. It’s important to remember that this is the victim’s choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer aliases, and stop using the victim's name once the sexual assault becomes the focus of the story unless permission is granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special care with incest cases to avoid revealing the victim's identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters need to exercise special care so that reporting the name of the perpetrator and the nature of the crime in incest cases does not thereby reveal the name of the victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider long-term online archive effects; prioritize protecting victims even if editors think locals already know names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic violence coverage: be cautious about portraying perpetrator who commits suicide as victim
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations that treat the perpetrator who commits suicide as a victim risk offending family and friends of the murder victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to how framing may re-victimize or offend survivors of the primary victim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunk driving coverage: do not minimize seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations such as MADD have helped dispel the myth that drunk driving is not a crime. Victims are upset when news accounts minimize cases of drunk driving that may have harmed others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that drunk driving is a potentially lethal crime and avoid language that downplays harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise special care with potentially vulnerable populations (children, elderly, disabled)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should exercise special care when interviewing people at both ends of the age spectrum. Some children are simply too young to be subjected to re-living their experiences during interviews without inflicting additional harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect untrained reporters to interview child victims; seek specialists and avoid leading children; accommodate elderly and disabled needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: News organizations should train rookie reporters on victim-sensitive reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of training and inexperience can mean rookies make mistakes that add stress and increase likelihood of secondary trauma. News organizations would be well advised to use this guide as a foundation for training rookies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement formal training for less-experienced staff who cover crime and consider incorporating this curriculum in journalism schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographers and videographers: avoid sensational, grisly, or clichéd images
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensational or grisly images often wound victims and their families; still photographs serve as a permanent record and clichés (body bag, coffin) can inflict pain without informing the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose visuals that inform rather than exploit; avoid gratuitous gore and repetitive clichéd imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow reporters to check headlines, corrections, and substantive changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editors change parts of stories, sometimes without conferring with reporters, which can result in errors or insensitivities. It is best to ensure that the system allows reporters who cover victims the opportunity to check headlines, corrections, and changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop workflows that let reporters verify sensitive edits before publication or airing where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize burden of 'pack journalism'; consider media pooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Confronting a horde of journalists outside a victim’s home is an unwelcome added stress. If staking out the victim’s home is unavoidable, news organizations should exercise special care to ensure their reporters’ presence does as little as possible to burden the victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a limited 'pool' of representatives to conduct interviews and share information with other media under agreed terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful that news values (speed, prominence, weirdness) can conflict with victim priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Three troubling news values are speed (competing to get the story first), prominence/celebrity (unequal coverage by status), and the 'weirdness' factor (seeking odd details). These can increase pressure, errors, and revictimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize accuracy over speed, equitable coverage beyond celebrity, and avoid highlighting odd or intimate details that would not be reported if the victim were a family member.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve cultural competency in coverage and newsroom diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Though newsrooms have made strides in recruiting, declines in revenues threaten progress. News organizations can teach reporters and editors specifics about diversity and cultural norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train reporters on culturally sensitive practices (e.g., eye contact norms, religious dress) and help bridge class/cultural divides to avoid marginalizing victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming anyone can cover anything without preparation; provide topic training
rubrics_metrics.description: Many organizations want reporters who can cover anything, but many reporters simply do not know much about crime and victimization. Reporters can grow up believing myths or half-truths that bias coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide targeted training to avoid misinformation and bias and to improve sensitivity in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider allowing victims to see stories prior to publication in some cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Some organizations allow verification of quotes but forbid advance copies of full stories. This rule may be reconsidered for victim coverage because minor mistakes or language can cause pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh allowing advance review for average citizens or victims to permit minor corrections that reduce harm without compromising coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disproportionate focus on the perpetrator; make victim stories compelling
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-profile case often emphasizes the perpetrator; for victims and their families this can be repugnant. The challenge is to find ways to make stories about victims equally compelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance narrative focus to elevate victims’ perspectives and dignity while still covering perpetrator-relevant facts responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide avenues for victims to hold news organizations accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: When victims have complaints about coverage, they may not know who is responsible. Sometimes the only redress is a letter to the editor. News organizations should offer proactive strategies to build mutually beneficial lines of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create clear complaint processes, designate contacts, and engage with victim advocates and service providers to improve accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize secondary victimization of journalists and offer support
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors can suffer from secondary trauma from exposure to disturbing scenes. Unaddressed, journalists risk unhealthy coping strategies and becoming hardened or insensitive to victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster a culture where journalists can discuss feelings, and provide support and counseling without fear that doing so will harm their careers.
